subject: Communication
title: News Avoidance: The Cost of Checking Out
description: A fast breakdown of News Avoidance: The Cost of Checking Out for builders.

hook.text: 36% of people worldwide actively avoid the news. After years of doom-scrolling, they simply disconnected.

buildup.text: News avoidance surged post-2020. Reuters Institute found exhaustion, anxiety, and helplessness driving people away.

discovery.text: Avoiding news reduces anxiety — but it also reduces civic awareness, preparedness, and informed decision-making.

twist.text: The answer isn't consume everything or consume nothing. It's consuming intentionally: curated sources, set times.

climax.text: A 'news diet' — deliberate, limited, diverse consumption — protects mental health while maintaining informed citizenship.

punchline.text: Don't drown in the news. Don't ignore it either. Sip it wisely.

quiz.question: What percentage of people worldwide actively avoid the news?

details.summary: News avoidance is the deliberate decision to stop following current events, driven by emotional exhaustion, distrust of media, and information overload. While understandable, it creates knowledge gaps that make citizens more vulnerable to misinformation and less able to participate in democracy.
details.whyItMatters: News avoidance is a rational response to problematic media, but it creates dangerous blind spots. The solution is better media habits, not withdrawal.
takeaways: News avoidance is growing, especially among younger demographics
It is driven by emotional exhaustion and media distrust

faq.question: Is it healthier to avoid news entirely?
faq.answer: Some reduction in news consumption can improve mental health, especially reducing doom scrolling. But complete avoidance creates vulnerability. The ideal is selective, intentional consumption from trusted sources at scheduled times rather than either constant connection or complete disconnection.

faq.question: How can news organizations address news avoidance?
faq.answer: By reducing sensationalism, providing context and solutions alongside problems, rebuilding trust through transparency about methods, and creating formats that respect audience time. Constructive journalism and explanatory journalism both show promising results in re-engaging avoidant audiences.
